articles.title: Morocco’s king appoints first woman prime minister in historic move
articles.summary: Morocco’s King Mohammed VI on Tuesday appointed Fatima Zahra Mansouri as the country’s first woman prime minister, marking a historic milestone in the
articles.body: Morocco’s King Mohammed VI on Tuesday appointed Fatima Zahra Mansouri as the country’s first woman prime minister, marking a historic milestone in the North African kingdom's political history.Mansouri, a 50-year-old lawyer who also served as the mayor of Marrakech and urban planning minister, has been tasked with forming a new government, the Royal Palace said in a statement. The appointment came four days after the announcement of parliamentary election results, according to the Associated Press (AP).Mansouri's Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) emerged as the largest party in the September 23 elections, securing 97 of the 395 seats in parliament, according to Morocco's Interior Ministry. The party will now have to negotiate with other political formations to secure a governing majority, as no single party won enough seats to govern independently.She becomes the second woman to serve as prime minister in the Arab world after Tunisia's Najla Bouden, who held the position between 2021 and 2023, AP reported.Coalition formation and economic challengesMansouri is expected to begin coalition negotiations in the coming days, with her administration facing the challenge of addressing economic concerns, including inflation, wages and employment, according to AP.Her government will also oversee billions of dollars in investments linked to preparations for the 2030 FIFA World Cup, which Morocco will co-host with Spain and Portugal, the news agency reported.Under Morocco's electoral system, the king appoints the head of government from the political party that secures the largest number of seats in the House of Representatives. However, the appointment does not give the party an automatic parliamentary majority, making coalition negotiations necessary, according to .The provision was introduced through Morocco's 2011 constitutional reforms following protests during the Arab Spring. The reforms linked the appointment of the head of government to the outcome of parliamentary elections, restricting the monarch's earlier discretion in selecting the prime minister. Al JazeeraMansouri's political backgroundMansouri joined PAM when it was founded in 2008 by Fouad Ali El Himma, a close adviser and longtime friend of King Mohammed VI. The party has positioned itself as a counterweight to the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD), advocating social modernisation and secular-leaning policies, reported.A French law graduate from the University of Montpellier, Mansouri rose through the party's ranks and became a prominent political figure. She has served as a member of parliament and twice as the mayor of Marrakech, while also holding the urban planning portfolio in the outgoing government, according to AP and .PAM victory and opposition partiesPAM's victory marks its first time emerging as the largest party in a parliamentary election since its establishment. It secured 97 seats, followed by the National Rally of Independents (RNI) with 66 seats and the Istiqlal Party with 65 seats, according to the final results announced by Morocco's Interior Ministry.The moderate Islamist Justice and Development Party secured 54 seats. Its leader and former prime minister Abdelilah Benkirane said the party would remain in opposition, reported.PAM's coalition-building efforts will take place against the backdrop of political dissatisfaction and declining voter participation. Turnout stood at approximately 38% of Morocco's 15.8 million registered voters, compared with around 50% in the 2021 parliamentary elections, according to .The election was held following youth-led protests in Morocco last year, which raised concerns over employment, healthcare and education, as well as the migration crisis involving attempts by migrants to enter the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in July, and Al Jazeera reported.You use AI every day. articles.body: TOI Correspondent from London: Diamond businessman Mehul Choksi has dropped a multi-million-pound London high court damages claim he was bringing against the Indian govt and a Hungarian woman named Barbara Jarabik, living in the UK, for allegedly kidnapping him in Antigua in a honeytrap plot on May 23, 2021.The Indian national (67), represented by Edward Fitzgerald KC, alleged at the HC that the Indian govt conspired with five individuals to unlawfully kidnap, torture and extrajudicially render him from Antigua to India, via Dominica, where he is accused of involvement in the £1.3 billion Punjab National Bank fraud. Choksi is in jail in Antwerp, where he is appealing a Belgian court’s extradition order to India.Earlier, Justice Mansfield had ordered that Choksi should pay security costs of £425,000 in respect of Gurdip Bath, now St Christopher and Nevis high commissioner to India, and Leslie Farrow-Guy, a British national and former driver of Bath, and £252,000 security costs in respect of Gurmit Singh, an Indian national, and Gurjit Singh Bhandal, a British Indian, for their legal costs should Choksi lose the case. “Much of the evidence relied on for this application is hearsay. There is no witness evidence as to the kidnapping and assault of the claimant, other than that of the claimant himself,” the judge had said.Choksi failed to pay the security to the court by the deadline, and so the claim was struck out against the four male defendants. “Subsequently, he has discontinued the case against the government of India and Jarabik,” 9BR Chambers, whose barrister, Gary Summers, represented Bath and Farrow-Guy, said.Choksi had claimed all five were living in the UK, where he alleges the conspiracy was hatched. articles.title: Soho House venue under investigation for food safety
articles.summary: A former chef contacted Hackney Council after complaining to managers at the members' club.
articles.body:
A venue of private members club Soho House is being investigated by the local council after a former member of staff raised concerns about rats and out-of-date food allegedly being served.

The former staff member told BBC News he was pressured replace labels on prepared food if it was not sold at the end of the day and said he regularly saw rats at the venue.

His contract was terminated two months after he first raised concerns, but Soho House said this was unrelated to his complaints.

It added that the food incident was isolated and re-labelling unsold food was not company policy, but it did not comment on the rats claim.

Hackney Council has confirmed it is investigating food safety and hygiene at Soho House's Shoreditch location.

Soho House is a popular haunt for A-list celebrities. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle reportedly had their first date at one of its London venues.

The former staff member at Shoreditch House, Kamran Khan, first raised concerns informally about the alleged re-labelling practice before formally filing a complaint with Soho House.

Khan was on probation at the venue when he raised the concerns in July, and his employment was terminated earlier in September.

Following his formal complaint, the company investigated and told Khan on 24 August there was evidence to support his claim and steps were being taken to address the matter.

Khan claimed the practice continued despite the assurances he was allegedly offered, leading him to complain to Hackney Council instead.

A spokesperson for the council said: "We have received a report about food safety and hygiene at Shoreditch House and have opened an investigation."

Speaking to BBC News, Khan said he was told in a probation meeting to continue the practice.

The 30-year-old, who told BBC News he has had several jobs in catering and hospitality said he was told "if I don't change labels on my own initiative, [they] would take that as a performance concern".

He said he felt compelled to raise the issue because he saw a lot of children and pregnant women at the restaurant.

"I told them that I don't want to be held personally liable for anyone that gets injured," he said.

Food served in a restaurant must legally be labelled with information including the best-before or use-by date.

Khan also said there had been rats at the venue for a long time and that cleaners were told to check daily for rat droppings.

A spokesperson for Soho House apologised for the incident, saying: "This is not how we expect our houses to operate and it is not company policy."

They said an external, independent investigation and audit was conducted.

"Delivering the highest level of food safety for our members and guests is incredibly important to us," they added.

"For clarity, the former employee's contract was terminated for reasons entirely unrelated to food labelling."

Soho House membership starts from £291.67 monthly or £204.17 for under-27s.

The group opened its first club in London in 1995, and now has 46 Soho Houses in Europe, North America and Asia, as well a string of other up-market hospitality businesses.

The company listed on the New York Stock Exchange in 2021, but its share price dropped sharply in the following years as it struggled to make a profit and fought accusations it was losing its exclusivity.

It was bought by a consortium of investors last year , with actor Ashton Kutcher joining the company's board.

articles.title: Chris Mason: Andy Burnham delivers deeply political speech with a personal core
articles.summary: The key thing to understand about Andy Burnham's speech is these were the words and the delivery of both a new prime minister and a grieving son, the BBC's political editor writes.
articles.body:
The key thing to understand about Andy Burnham's speech is these were the words and the delivery of both a new prime minister and a grieving son.

Burnham is living through two life-shaping, even life-defining moments right now – becoming and adjusting to being prime minister during the final weeks of his dad Roy's life, and preparing his speech while dealing with the grief of his loss.

The funeral will take place in a few days' time.

Reflections on his dad's life and influence formed the personal spine to this deeply political speech, which ranged far and wide.

Labour figures are enthused that they now have a leader with what they see as a clear sense of purpose that can be easily articulated.

The tacit, unflattering comparison with former PM Sir Keir Starmer is obvious .

Burnham vows to end existing pension triple lock in 2030 to help fund care

Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system

Burnham says public body will invest in electricity grid

What stood out in this speech was its breadth. His pitch could, very broadly, be divided into the short term - what he hopes to achieve before a general election; and the long term - the prospectus he is beginning to assemble to put to the country when polling day comes around inside the next three years.

The biggest ideas have the longest timeframe and, perhaps, the greatest need for a lengthy debate in their gestation.

Take the headline grabber: revamping social care in England. Previous attempts to do so, by both Labour and the Conservatives, haven't survived the intensity of a general election campaign, having been announced close to an election.

The aim of Burnham's plan is to seed a conversation now about what a new system might look like – the idea being that the argument is won in advance.

Let's see. The debate is only just beginning.

The plan to fund this by making increases in the state pension from 2030 less generous than they are now was more detailed than some expected at this stage.

The triple lock means the state pension currently increases annually in line with inflation, average wage growth or 2.5%, whichever is highest.

But from April 2030, if Labour win the next election, the annual earnings link will be dropped. It would, Labour figures say, be increased further if needed, to ensure that it stays above 30% of the full time average wage.

Knowing they would face blunt criticism about binning the existing triple lock – note the reaction of the Unite union and Labour's political rivals – it would appear the prime minister was keen to offer as much of what he hopes will be reassuring detail to many.

Also going into the next Labour manifesto, he said, a change in the Westminster voting system and – after a review to come – the idea of a closer relationship with the European Union.

How much closer, with what trade offs and prompting what reaction, we don't yet know.

And from the longer term stuff to the here and now – including housing reform in England, more public control of the water industry and the electricity grid.

There was an energy and sense of urgency to Burnham's pitch and without question he has created a battalion of dividing lines with Labour's political opponents which are likely to dominate the debate ahead.

His cabinet and many in his party are relishing the battle of ideas the prime minister has set up and is enthusiastically leaning into.

It was noteworthy that beyond a broad reference to Labour's opponents on the Right, the party's rivals didn't get a mention in a speech lasting more than an hour.

The question is: does he and his government have the capacity to deliver?

And do they have the capacity to convince you, the voter, they have a vision you regard as coherent, appealing and affordable?

You hardly need reminding of the backdrop that contributed to thwarting many of his recent, many predecessors: a persistently sclerotic economy and a persistently turbulent international picture, for starters.

Neither will make turning all of this into a reality straightforward.

articles.title: Trump’s border wall construction cut into an ancient ground carving older than Stonehenge
articles.summary: The Las Playas intaglio carving of a huge fish is  at least two thousand  years older than the first Egyptian pyramid, according to researchers’ recent estimations.
articles.body: An ancient ground carving that was severely damaged by the administration’s border wall construction was created before Stonehenge and Egypt’s oldest pyramid, according to recently publicized research. The Las Playas Intaglio, a giant fish carved into the Sonoran Desert in Arizona, is now considered the oldest example in the Americas of a geoglyphic, the ancient art form that is carved into or drawn on the ground. In April, contractors hired by the Trump administration to make way for a second wall along the Arizona-Mexico border “scraped” a 50-foot swath through the ancient carving, according to the Center for Biological Diversity, which documented the damage. The intaglio on the ground of the ancestral homeland of the Tohono O’odham and other Indigenous tribes is estimated to be about 2,000 years older than Egypt’s first pyramid and to have been created about 1,500 years before the first construction of Stonehenge and 4,000 years before Peru’s Nazca Lines, researchers have found. The formerly 272-foot carving had originally been thought to be about 1,000 years old. But the latest research dates the art’s creation to at least 6,500 years ago, and possibly as much as 7,500 years ago. That age emphasizes “the significance of this site and the parallel great misfortune resulting from its damage,” the researchers said in an article published in The SAA Archaeological Record. “This discovery makes an already devastating loss even more profound. It’s a cultural and historical atrocity,” Russ McSpadden, Southwest conservation advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity, said in a statement. A Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said in an email to NBC News that the contractor “inadvertently disturbed” the site and that CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott has been “engaged directly with tribal leadership to determine appropriate next steps.” “The remaining portion of the site has been secured and will be protected in place. CBP is conducting a thorough review of construction protocols and strengthening communication procedures to ensure this does not happen again,” the spokesperson stated, adding that the agency is “committed to respecting and safeguarding cultural heritage throughout all border infrastructure projects.” The damage to that site and construction on other parts of Tohono O’odham land and sacred Indigenous areas has strained the tenuous relationship between the tribal nation and the government. The tribe is appealing a federal judge’s decision refusing to block the administration’s border wall construction through its reservation. While the intaglio’s site is irreparably damaged, the Tohono O’odham people are trying to stop the government from plowing through Quitobaquito Springs, a desert water source in Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument that is also considered a sacred site and holds endangered species. In order to build the border wall and barriers, the Department of Homeland Security invoked authority granted in the Secure Fence Act of 2006 to waive numerous laws protecting the environment, water, cultural, historical and religious sites. The Tohono O’odham Nation has long worked with CBP, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security, on border security, helping to keep drug traffickers and others from using its land for criminal activity. The tribe’s reservation straddles the U.S.-Mexico border, and its members have permission to move between the two countries with ID checks. About 3,000 of its members are in Mexico, according to the tribal nation. The Center for Biological Diversity stated in a news release that conservation advocates and tribal nations have long warned that border wall and secondary border barrier plans could cut through sensitive habitat and cultural sites across the region. Wall construction in other parts of the border has sparked other lawsuits and opposition from landowners, Native American tribes, local governments, conservation groups, business owners and others. In Texas, a tribal nonprofit for the Lipan Apache and an outdoor recreation business have opposed the border wall construction, alleging DHS is not authorized to violate the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, which they say it would do by destroying or cutting off access to sacred sites. A federal judge ordered a temporary halt to construction in Big Bend National Park in response to the lawsuit, but construction continues on other parts of the rugged, undeveloped and remote region outside state and federal parkland.

articles.title: In the early 1970s, David Wolkowsky began stewarding a remote island near Key West and hosted famous guests there; decades later the 14-acre Ballast Key became part of a national wildlife refuge
articles.summary: A private 14-acre island nine miles west of Key West that once hosted famous writers and Hollywood stars has officially become part of the Key West
articles.body: A private 14-acre island nine miles west of Key West that once hosted famous writers and Hollywood stars has officially become part of the Key West National Wildlife Refuge. The move completes a conservation effort that lasted for decades. Known as Ballast Key, the remote tropical island was bought in the early 1970s by the late property developer David Wolkowsky. For almost half a century, Wolkowsky looked after the isolated retreat. He built a three-storey main house and a separate guest house surrounded by palm trees and shallow turquoise water. The deal was made possible through a partnership between The Nature Conservancy and the US Fish and Wildlife Service, as detailed by the Miami Herald. The purchase means the last privately owned piece of land within the national wildlife sanctuary boundary is now permanently protected from commercial development.A private sanctuary for literary legendsOver the years, Wolkowsky turned the empty island into a well-known haven for artists. Known in South Florida as "Mr Key West," he often welcomed famous writers, musicians and performers looking for a quiet place away from public attention. One of his regular guests was playwright Tennessee Williams. During the late 1970s, Williams spent long periods on the island painting watercolours on its wooden wraparound porches. Author Truman Capote, musician Jimmy Buffett, and members of the Rockefeller and Vanderbilt families also stayed there as Wolkowsky's guests. According to historical archives published by The Nature Conservancy, the island also appeared in popular culture. It was used as a villain's hideout in the 1989 James Bond film Licence to Kill. Author John Gardner also included Ballast Key in the novelisation of the film. To make the remote property comfortable for his guests, Wolkowsky installed custom solar power systems and a private desalination plant. The plant turned seawater into fresh drinking water. Building materials and supplies were regularly carried across the open channel on a private barge sent from Key West.Protecting critical wildlife habitatsBallast Key is important not only for its cultural history but also for its place in the Florida Keys marine ecosystem. The island lies within the Great White Heron and Key West National Wildlife Refuges. It provides important nesting and feeding areas for dozens of rare bird species. Biologists from the US Fish and Wildlife Service said the island's sandy beaches and nearby shallow tidal flats are home to nesting brown pelicans, magnificent frigatebirds, roseate spoonbills and sea turtles. The surrounding seagrass beds provide shelter for wading birds, nurse sharks and bonefish. Under the land transfer reported by the Miami Herald, The Nature Conservancy first acquired the property before transferring it to the federal government. The agreement fulfilled Wolkowsky's stated wish that the island remain undeveloped after his death in 2018 at the age of 99. To support long-term conservation research, federal officials assigned the existing homes and other structures for administrative and scientific use. The buildings now provide accommodation for visiting marine biologists, wildlife researchers and university scholars studying climate resilience across the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary.The legacy of Mr Key WestWolkowsky's care of Ballast Key was part of a wider commitment to historic preservation and environmental protection across Monroe County. Born in Key West in 1919, Wolkowsky spent decades restoring historic buildings in the city centre. This included turning a run-down waterfront property into the Pier House resort during the late 1960s. Local historians credit his building projects with helping change Key West from a quiet naval outpost into a global tourist destination while protecting its distinct local character. Speaking to the Miami Herald after the land transfer, representatives from The Nature Conservancy said Wolkowsky's vision had protected the unique island environment from future resort development. The permanent addition of Ballast Key to the federal refuge system ensures that the southernmost piece of privately owned land in the contiguous United States will remain a protected wilderness area for the future.You use AI every day. articles.title: Puja ticket sale scam: ED raids homes of ex-minister Indranil Sen, relatives
articles.summary: ED raids ex-tourism minister and singer Indranil Sen’s homes, probes alleged Durga Puja “preview pass” sales via massArt; Rs 50–60 crore irregularities suspected.
articles.body: Kolkata/Singur: Enforcement Directorate (ED) on Tuesday raided two homes of singer Indranil Sen, who was a junior tourism minister in the erstwhile Trinamool govt, and many other addresses in connection with complaints of corruption linked to the alleged sale of Durga Puja “preview passes”.ED officials searched 15 addresses in Kolkata and Hooghly, including Sen’s homes in Kasba and near Singur, and homes of his relatives.An apartment in Highland Park, owned by a businessman involved in event management, was among the addresses searched.Sen has been summoned to ED’s Salt Lake office at 11am on Wednesday.The raids were linked to a police probe against the singer and his wife, Madhuchhanda, following a complaint lodged by travel agent Jaydip Mukherjee.Sen’s wife is associated with an organisation called ‘massArt’, which works towards “promoting art and culture of Bengal”.Set up in June 2022, ‘massArt’ had allegedly showcased a tie-up with Unesco and sold “preview passes” for select Durga Puja pandals.When asked about the ED raids, CM Suvendu Adhikari said, “Indranil Sen used to take a cut from singers’ payments”. BJP refused to comment on the case.An anticipatory bail petition moved by Sen and his wife is pending at Calcutta HC. Sources said “preview passes” for 24 Durga Puja pandals in Kolkata were sold through massArt at prices ranging between Rs 1,749 and Rs 5,499. “massArt was running a cartel in Unesco’s name. They selected 24 pujas and sold tickets for entering those pandals. None other than those having tickets were allowed to enter the pandals during that period (before the pandals were opened to the general public),” said Jaydip Mukherjee, who filed the police complaint.“They claimed Unesco was their partner. I had sent an email to Unesco in 2023. They called me up on Sept 23, 2025, and denied having any partnership with massArt for selecting pandals,” said Mukherjee, who appeared before ED on Sept 17.The sources said the investigators suspect that around 19,000 passes were sold in 2022, 34,000 in 2023 and 61,000 in 2024. ED suspects financial irregularities of Rs 50 crore to Rs 60 crore linked to the sale of “preview passes”.Earlier, Sen had claimed that police had found no financial record, balance sheet or audit report to back the allegations of financial irregularities. articles.title: 'American Idol' alum Caleb Flynn convicted of murdering his wife
articles.summary: Alleigha Botner's testimony revealed 107,000 messages with Caleb Flynn, including chilling texts sent just hours before Ashley Flynn was killed.
articles.body: Former "American Idol" contestant Caleb Flynn was convicted Tuesday of murdering his wife, Ashley Flynn, following an Ohio trial that exposed his secret affair and a series of messages about wanting his wife dead. Flynn was found guilty on all counts. DAD OF 'AMERICAN IDOL' CONTESTANT'S SLAIN WIFE MADE EERIE GOOGLE SEARCH AFTER HEARING OF HER MURDER Flynn faced nine charges: one count of aggravated murder, three counts of murder, two counts of felonious assault and three counts of tampering with evidence involving the missing firearm, the side garage door and emails. articles.title: CWG setback fuels Parul’s Asian Games comeback
articles.summary: Parul Chaudhary rebounds from CWG disappointment to win Asian Games bronze in 5000m (15:14.61) and steeplechase; debutant Jay Kumar takes two 4x400m relay medals.
articles.body: Lucknow: A month after the disappointment at the Commonwealth Games, Uttar Pradesh Police DSP Parul Chaudhary has scripted a powerful comeback on the Asian stage, proving that one poor outing could not define her hard work.Parul, one of India’s most consistent distance runners, clinched two medals at the ongoing Asian Games, including a bronze in the women’s 5000m final. She clocked 15:14.61 to finish behind Bahrain’s Winfred Yavi, who took gold in 15:10.18, and Japan’s Nozomi Tanaka, who claimed silver in 15:11.65.The medal added to Parul’s earlier bronze in the women’s 3000m steeplechase, making it a memorable campaign for the Meerut-born athlete, who has balanced her sporting career with her responsibilities as a DSP in Uttar Pradesh Police.Speaking to TOI from Nagoya, Parul said the Commonwealth Games setback forced her to reassess her preparation and return stronger.“The Commonwealth Games were a major setback for me. Between the Commonwealth Games and the Asian Games, I worked on correcting my mistakes, focused on improving my jumps and speed, and prepared myself for strong competition within a month,” Parul said.Her turnaround was built on intense technical work, sharper race planning and mental recovery. In the 3000m steeplechase, Parul had to deal with world-class athletes from Bahrain and Kazakhstan. In the 5000m, she faced a field packed with strong runners from Japan, Bahrain and Kazakhstan.“I knew I would face tough rivals in both the 3000m steeplechase and the 5000m. In the 5000m, my main competitors were from Japan, Bahrain and Kazakhstan, while in the 3000m steeplechase, the strongest athletes were from Bahrain and Kazakhstan, including world and Olympic-level champions,” she said.“I am very happy that I won these medals for the country. I feel proud to have won medals for India at such a big stage. I am grateful to the country and my state for supporting athletes like us. Now, it is our duty to continue winning medals for the nation,” she said.Her focus now shifts to bigger global targets — the World Athletics Championships and the Los Angeles Olympics — as she looks to build on a comeback that took shape in just one month.Debutant Jay makes mark with twin medalsAsian Games debutant Jay Kumar enjoyed a memorable outing in Nagoya, winning two medals for India in the 4x400m relay events.The 21-year-old athlete from Gautam Budh Nagar clinched a bronze medal in the men’s 4x400m relay and a silver medal in the mixed 4x400m relay at the Asian Games.India’s men’s 4x400m relay team, comprising Dharmveer Choudhary, Manu Thekkinalil, Jay Kumar and Vishal Thennarasu, produced a strong performance in the final on Tuesday to finish third. The quartet clocked 3:01.61 in a closely contested race, with less than a second separating the top three teams.Speaking to TOI from Nagoya, Jay Kumar said he was delighted to win two medals in his first Asian Games appearance.“I am extremely happy that in my very first event at the Asian Games, I won two medals. articles.title: Israel kills senior Hamas commander in Gaza strike
articles.summary: An Israeli airstrike killed the head of Hamas’ armed wing in north Gaza on Tuesday, officials on both sides said, with the militant group describing him as a ⁠leader of the Oct.
articles.body: An Israeli airstrike killed the head of Hamas’ armed wing in north Gaza on Tuesday, officials on both sides said, with the militant group describing him as a ⁠leader of the Oct. 7, 2023 attack that precipitated war in the Palestinian enclave. Israel’s government said its military had targeted and killed Izz al-Din Al-Beik, who they said was involved in planning attacks and recruiting. Hamas confirmed his death. Medics said the Israeli strike hit an apartment building in Gaza City’s Nasr neighborhood around dawn. A second person died from wounds after the attack, health officials ⁠said. Later on Tuesday, an Israeli airstrike near a medical clinic in ​Jabalia ⁠refugee camp killed one person, taking the day’s death toll to at least three, medics said. The military said it had targeted a militant in the area. Israel, which says Hamas has been rearming ⁠and launching attacks in violation of an October ceasefire, has stepped up strikes on the group in recent weeks. The ​Israeli ⁠military says it has killed at least ‌20 Hamas figures this month, including some it identified as senior commanders, people who took part in the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks or those who held Israeli hostages. Hamas has denied trying to carry out attacks or rebuild its arsenal ‌and accuses Israel of undermining the Gaza peace deal. Mass funeral Also on ‌Tuesday, Palestinians in the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza buried the remains of 41 people killed by Israeli fire nearly three years ago. Their bodies were recently recovered from ruins. Hundreds of relatives and friends gathered in an open space to pay respect as the remains were placed ⁠in white shrouds decorated by Palestinian flags. “There are mixed feelings between relief, sadness, and pain. But thank God, the fire in my heart has eased a little, because my husband now has a grave that my orphaned children and I can visit,” said Areej Farajallah, who lost her husband in the Oct. 31, 2023 strike. Palestinian authorities estimate more than 8,000 bodies remain buried in wreckage. A Palestinian recovery team that combed wreckage in Gaza City last month said it found the remains of 112 people from the same clan. “With minimal equipment, their remains were recovered after hours of ‌work, retrieving what was left of bones, some skulls, and hair with which it is extremely difficult ​for us to identify them,” said Rami Al-Ayedi, of Gaza’s Civil Defense Service. Last year’s U.S.-brokered ceasefire ‌calls for eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little ⁠progress has been made as negotiators have failed to agree terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel ⁠to withdraw its troops. Israeli airstrikes have continued. At least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire, according to the territory’s health officials, while ‌Israel says four soldiers have ​been killed. Palestinian authorities say more than 73,000 people have been ‌killed in Israel’s assault on Gaza, launched after Hamas-led ​fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel in October 2023.

articles.title: 15k Ladakh-grown Liliums set out for national flower markets
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: The first consignment of Ladakh-grown Lilium flowers was dispatched to major flower markets in India on Tuesday, in what the Union Territory
articles.body: SRINAGAR: The first consignment of Ladakh-grown Lilium flowers was dispatched to major flower markets in India on Tuesday, in what the Union Territory administration called a major step towards boosting new economic opportunities and entrepreneurship in the cold desert.The consignment comprised 15,000 red, pink, white, and orange Lilium blooms cultivated at an altitude of 10,600ft at the world’s highest flower field at Choglamsar, Leh. These “A-grade” Liliums have four to five buds on each stem and fetch a premium price of around Rs 150-200 in retail markets. The flowers, with a shelf life of five to seven days, will be sold in various domestic markets, primarily Delhi, Mumbai, and Chandigarh.Ladakh lieutenant governor Vinai Kumar Saxena, who flagged off the consignment at Leh airport, said: “This first-of-its-kind high-altitude commercial floriculture project in Ladakh represents a major agricultural and visual shift for the region, which has, since ages, been identified by its rugged mountains and barren valleys. Millions of Liliums have added a vibrant contrast to this dull landscape.”Saxena said the “historic” initiative had emerged as a powerful economic tool for creating alternative sustainable livelihoods in Ladakh. Fifteen women cut, sort and package the flowers at these fields for a daily wage of Rs 900 each. A young, qualified botanist markets the produce to flower markets across the nation. The employees are all locals.The UT administration has directed deputy commissioners of Kargil, Drass, Sham, Changthang and Zanskar districts to replicate the high-altitude floriculture model by identifying at least 20 acres of land in each district.The flower field in Leh, which houses more than 25 lakh blooms, was developed and readied within just two months. It was opened to the public on Sept 17 this year and has since received an overwhelming response from visitors.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

Gen-Z — of which I am a member — have forgone the wallet in favor of back-of-phone cardholders, wristlets, or just sticking with Apple Pay. Not only are these alternatives convenient, they’re also less bulky and much easier to grab and go than traditional wallets. articles.title: BJP asks chief secy to ‘throw away’ statehood resolution, says it will strain Centre-J&K ties
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: A day after the Jammu & Kashmir assembly passed a resolution seeking restoration of statehood with a reference to autonomy, leader of opposition
articles.body: SRINAGAR: A day after the Jammu & Kashmir assembly passed a resolution seeking restoration of statehood with a reference to autonomy, leader of opposition Sunil Sharma said the move would strain Centre-J&K relations and urged chief secretary Atal Dulloo not to forward the resolution to the Union govt. The BJP member also demanded speaker Abdul Rahim Rather’s resignation and claimed that Union home minister Amit Shah was unhappy about the resolution.“Already the chief secretary and the law secretary gave their opinion to the assembly that they cannot discuss the resolution as the issue is sub judice. Their communication to the assembly secretariat ahead of the resolution is an indication that the resolution is anti-Constitution. We expect the chief secretary not to forward the resolution to the Centre and throw it away,” Sharma told TOI.Sources said the assembly secretariat had sent the resolution to the chief secretary to be forwarded to the Centre.NC legislator Justice (retired) Hasnain Masoodi said the assembly secretariat should have directly sent it to the central govt instead of routing it through the chief secretary, as he had objected to the resolution.The assembly Monday adopted the resolution that seeks restoration of statehood amid protests and a walkout by BJP legislators, who accused NC and Congress of being anti-national over the reference to the autonomy resolution passed in the House in 2000.The chief secretary and the law secretary are facing criticism from the National Conference and other parties for writing to the assembly secretariat earlier, advising against taking up the resolution.Speaking in the House on Monday, CM Omar Abdullah, who moved the resolution, said he was also the law minister and was not even aware “that my law secretary is sending you opinions”.Sharma defended the two bureaucrats, saying they had expressed the “right opinion” as the resolution, he claimed, was “anti-constitutional” and “anti-national”.He said the speaker not only allowed the resolution to be introduced but also permitted amendments referring to autonomy and condemning the abrogation of Article 370, which was upheld by the Supreme Court. “The speaker has to step down,” he added. BJP has already moved a motion in the assembly against Rather.Sharma said the Centre was unhappy over the resolution as it would encourage separatism in J&K. “I met the (Union) home minister (Amit Shah) on Sunday. He expressed displeasure over the resolution,” Sharma said.According to Sharma, Shah told him during the meeting in New Delhi that statehood would be restored to J&K at an “appropriate time”, but anything that could disturb the peaceful situation would not be allowed.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: New York attorney general to review Cornell’s response to rape allegations as local DA reopens investigation
articles.summary: A former Cornell University student filed a lawsuit this month alleging she was drugged and gang raped inside a fraternity house in 2024, and the fresh scrut...
articles.body:
A former Cornell University student filed a lawsuit this month alleging she was drugged and gang raped inside a fraternity house in 2024, and the fresh scrutiny has prompted local prosecutors to reopen the investigation and the state attorney general to start a review of the school's initial response to the allegations.

The 101-page lawsuit details disturbing allegations about what the woman, identified as Jane Doe, says unfolded inside Chi Phi's frat house the night of October 19, 2024, and how the university and local prosecutors in Ithaca, New York, handled the case. Doe is accusing seven members of the frat of participating in the assault while she was unable to consent.

The Tompkins County District Attorney's Office said Monday it reopened the case to seek a grand jury review after being "asked by the community to revisit the decision whether to pursue criminal charges against the seven fraternity members."

County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said no criminal charges were initially filed because Doe had not provided Cornell police in 2024 with the same key allegations outlined in the new lawsuit.

Doe's attorney says the information was promptly given to Cornell authorities, and the report was "not materially different from what is contained in the (2026) complaint."

The legal dispute, lack of criminal charges and university's response has prompted fierce backlash and revived concerns about how schools respond to allegations of campus sexual assault.

The office of New York Attorney General Letitia James, meanwhile, is reviewing Cornell University's response to the rape allegations, a spokesman for the office said Tuesday.

Lawsuit alleges hours-long gang rape advertised in frat group text

The complaint names more than a dozen defendants, including the seven fraternity members from 2024, Cornell University and the Chi Phi fraternity. Allegations include negligence, breach of contract, sexual assault and battery, and violations of New York's Human Rights Law.

CNN has sought comment from several named parties in the lawsuit.

The complaint says Doe was 20 and had been drinking at her sorority house and a bar before she arrived at the Chi Phi house to visit a friend, who was one of the fraternity members, on the night of October 19, 2024.

According to the suit, Doe had already consumed about 10 standard drinks within the previous three hours when she arrived at the fraternity house.

The complaint alleges the friend and another fraternity member gave her more alcohol and pressured her into snorting a substance they described as ketamine, and that she was then sexually assaulted while "incapable of consent." A third fraternity member eventually entered the room and also sexually assaulted her, the complaint alleges.

At roughly 1:42 a.m., one of the men allegedly sent a message to the fraternity's Snapchat group chat a message – titled "Chi Phi Actives" – stating there was "free p*ssy" upstairs.

By doing this, the suit alleges, one of the accused "encouraged other … chapter members to join in on the gang rape of plaintiff."

A photo of a portion of the chat is included in the filing. Multiple fraternity members then entered the room, where one of the newcomers kissed her without her consent, and one of the first three men commanded her to take more ketamine and groped her, according to the complaint.

The seven defendants in the complaint poured ketamine onto her body and snorted it, the complaint says.

Eventually, five defendants left the room, and the remaining two men led her to a different room, where those two instructed her to take more ketamine and sexually assaulted her until about 5:45 a.m., the complaint says.

An attorney for one of the accused fraternity brothers denied any wrongdoing by his client.

"Even the district attorney's office, led by a chief prosecutor with the duty to pursue justice and uphold the rule of law without bias or favor, filed no charges against (him) because what she alleged did not happen," attorney Jeremy Saland said in a statement to CNN. He said his client "never sexually assaulted or even touched the plaintiff in any way."

An attorney for a different student gave ABC News a statement acknowledging that student participated in the Snapchat conversation mentioned in the complaint but denying that he engaged in sexual activity.

"I did not participate in any sexual activity or drug use. I was not found responsible by Cornell for any of the accusations involving sexual activity and drug use for which others received serious consequences," the student said through his attorney. "I thoughtlessly engaged in Snapchat and briefly stopped in the room where misconduct happened but not when it happened."

CNN is working to determine whether the other fraternity brothers have representation.

Chi Phi declined to discuss the specific allegations, citing pending litigation, but said it "unequivocally condemns sexual violence."

"Our founding principles of Truth, Honor, and Personal Integrity, and our mission of Building Better Men, call on every brother to demonstrate character through his actions and respect for the dignity and safety of others," the national fraternity said in a release. "Sexual violence is fundamentally incompatible with those expectations."

District attorney says Doe's 2024 statement varies from new lawsuit

The district attorney said the report Jane Doe made to university police differs significantly from the allegations in the lawsuit.

Nothing in Doe's original statement indicated she was drugged without consent or had sex against her will, Van Houten said. According to the accuser's statement, "each time Jane Doe asked to stop the sexual conduct, the sexual conduct stopped."

Van Houten's office has not released the full police report. CNN has asked Doe's attorney for a response to Van Houten's statement and for a copy of her complete 2024 police statement.

During a contentious interview Monday, CNN's Jake Tapper pressed Van Houten on why there wasn't a more expansive investigation from law enforcement or the DA's office after the report was made in 2024.

"We can't change what happened in the past as much as the community is outraged," Van Houten said. "My job under the New York State Constitution is to apply the penal law of New York state. We are constrained by that law. Whether you agree with it, whether you think someone's conduct is morally repugnant or vulgar or disgusting. I'm still constrained by the law."

The district attorney doubled down on that argument Tuesday.

"Jane Doe told us through her six-page written statement (in 2024) what happened," Van Houten told CNN's Pamela Brown. "When you know that very detailed, comprehensive account does not establish a crime, it's not ethical for a prosecutor or for the police to go out and look for or cross-examine her to find evidence of a crime."

Van Houten on Monday acknowledged that the text message screenshots between the men "were completely vulgar and disgusting, but they had nothing to do with her consent."

Tapper asked when Van Houten got copies of the text messages, included in the complaint, that the fraternity brothers sent each other.

Van Houten said that his team did not see the text messages evidence initially.

"They were not part of our initial analysis, but I understand that Cornell had them, and they sent them to our team," he said.

Earlier, Doe's attorney, Thomas P. Giuffra, said in a release that he believes the initial investigation was inadequate.

"It is challenging for me to understand how a thorough criminal investigation could have been conducted when she never spoke with anyone other than the officer who took her original complaint," Giuffra said.

"Other than her initial contact with Cornell police, she was not contacted by investigators from the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office or any investigators trained in interviewing rape survivors," Giuffra said.

"If the district attorney's office is now considering prosecution, I believe that it is a step in the right direction, albeit a late one."

Van Houten hopes to begin, by Wednesday, a process of speaking with Doe "to understand what insights she's gained over the last two years, what additional reflections and healing that she's done that she can provide to us in terms of additional evidence that we could present to the grand jury," he said Tuesday. He said he's been in contact with her attorney.

The Ithaca Police Department said Monday that it was "disturbed" to hear about the 2024 allegations. The department noted it learned about the alleged incident only recently through the media and said the incident was not reported to the agency.

In a statement Tuesday, a Cornell University spokesperson told CNN campus police investigated the incident in 2024 and consulted the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office, "which is the established protocol if it believes it is possible a crime has occurred."

Complaint faults Cornell for failing to discipline the accused

Doe reported the incident to Cornell University police on November 8, 2024, the complaint says.

Doe's attorney said Cornell expelled two of the seven accused students while the others received lesser punishment, including suspensions, workshops or written assignments.

Cornell countered that claim Monday, saying there was a range of sanctions for the accused students, including suspensions and expulsions. But "none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement," the university said.

In a September 21 statement, Cornell declined to confirm the individual disciplinary outcomes, citing federal student privacy law. The school said violations of university policy "could lead to sanctions up to and including suspension or expulsion," adding, "We will respond in detail through the legal process."

The sanctions came after it conducted a formal Title IX investigation, separate from the criminal proceeding, and a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days, the school said.

The school also said it had closed the chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity, and that the chapter remains barred from campus.

The lawsuit faults Cornell for failing to properly discipline after the assault, "all the while sheltering them from speaking to law enforcement, and silencing victims."

Cornell's "conduct was so outrageous, shocking, despicable, and contemptible that it exceeds the reasonable bounds of decency as measured by what the average member of the community would tolerate and demonstrates an utter disregard for the consequences that would follow," the lawsuit says.

The complaint is seeking a jury trial to determine monetary damages.

Cornell said Monday it "supports the decision of the Tompkins County District Attorney (DA) to provide an opportunity for the victim's story … to be heard by a criminal grand jury."

"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," Cornell said in a release. "A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault."

As for the review of Cornell's response by the state attorney general's office: Given the early stages of the review, it is unclear what actions, if any, the office could take against Cornell as the local district attorney's office reopens its investigation.

Earlier this year, James' office launched an investigation into Columbia University for its handling of allegations against a former university gynecologist who continued to work at one of the university's hospitals weeks after he was arrested on sex crimes charges . James' investigation looked at school officials' conduct in the weeks following the gynecologist's arrest.

A growing backlash and calls for accountability

The lawsuit — along with a lack of criminal charges and accusations of inadequate discipline — has drawn a wave of outrage.

Cornell student Hayden Watkins, executive vice president of the Student Assembly, said many students are talking about the allegations and the feeling on campus is "pretty grim."

"I think a lot of people are upset about it knowing that it happened on campus, and truthfully I think a lot of people feel not enough was done," Watkins said.

Ithaca Mayor Robert G. Cantelmo on Monday called for a pause on Cornell University's Greek life and student group gatherings.

The mayor said on Instagram that the moratorium would be in place "until such time that the University conducts an accounting of its protocols to prevent and prosecute crimes of sexual violence and publicly releases new standards and practices to keep our community safe."

A Cornell spokesperson said the university "shares the mayor's interest in student well-being and safety," and that the university "will work with him to address his concerns."

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul called the allegations "horrifying," and said she supported the district attorney's decision to reopen the criminal investigation.

"No student should ever be left wondering whether the institutions meant to protect them will listen and act," she said in a release.

She also called for outside counsel to conduct an independent review of the university's response, saying there are "serious questions about Cornell's campus culture and its systems for prevention, reporting, and response."

US Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a Democrat from New York City, condemned what she described as a "culture of rape" at elite universities and institutions during a Sunday town hall in Ithaca.

"Those men posted in a group chat," Ocasio-Cortez said , referencing allegations in the lawsuit. "That means it was normal to them, that means it was acceptable to them. This is a culture, this is norms, these are practices, and what we must do is understand that we cannot protect those spaces anymore."

"What about the life that those girls then have to endure, with the knowledge that his reputation is more precious than her truth?" she added.

articles.title: A Pennsylvania dairy farmer spent 70 years watching bears and turkeys on his 170-acre farm; in 2026, after turning down two lucrative offers, he permanently protected the land from development
articles.summary: After spending most of his life on the same Pennsylvania farm, dairy farmer Jeff Biddle has chosen to protect it from development, even after receiving
articles.body: After spending most of his life on the same Pennsylvania farm, dairy farmer Jeff Biddle has chosen to protect it from development, even after receiving two lucrative offers from potential buyers. The 170-acre Bear Meadows Farm near Tussey Mountain was placed under a permanent conservation easement in July 2026, according to the Centre County Farmland Trust. The conservation group WeConservePA also reported the preservation in August, while earlier reporting by Penn State Student Media documented Biddle’s long-standing connection to the farm and his work as a dairy farmer. The decision means the property can continue to be farmed, but its development rights are permanently restricted. The easement is attached to the property deed, so the protection remains in place even if ownership changes in the future.A farm that became part of a family’s lifeBiddle’s connection to Bear Meadows began in childhood. His father, Harold, purchased the property in 1959 after first acquiring woodland for a hunting camp. He restored the farm’s buildings and ran a beef operation there.Jeff eventually left to work as a cabinet-maker and ran his own woodworking business, but farming remained part of his life. He and his wife, Claudia, eventually took over the operation in 2002. Biddle had wanted to run a dairy farm since he was young. The family converted Bear Meadows into a grass-based dairy in 2005, and the farm received permission to sell raw milk in Pennsylvania in 2009.The farm now produces raw milk, eggs and grass-fed beef, while milk from its herd is also used to make a range of cheeses by an off-site cheesemaker. The farm’s website says it has been selling raw milk to customers in the State College area since 2009.Biddle’s approach to farming has also been documented by Penn State Student Media, their feauture described a demanding daily routine involving milking cows, caring for chickens and serving customers who came directly to the farm.Two offers could have changed the landscapeBiddle had been considering conservation for roughly three decades. During that period, he turned down two offers from buyers interested in the property. For him, the issue was not simply the financial value of the land. Development would have changed the fields, woods and views that had defined the farm throughout his life.The conservation easement now makes that change far less likely. Houses and other forms of development cannot replace the agricultural landscape protected under the agreement. That distinction is important because Bear Meadows sits near the Centre Region’s growth boundary, an area where development pressure and open land meet.The land protects more than farmlandThe preservation also has implications beyond agriculture. According to the Centre County Farmland Trust, Bear Meadows contains pasture, hay fields, cultivated cropland, forest and grassland. Its wooded areas include deciduous, evergreen and mixed forests, while streams and springs on the property feed into the wider Spring Creek watershed.The property includes a historic spring house and several waterways that eventually connect to Spring Creek. That water system forms part of a larger watershed extending toward the Susquehanna River and ultimately the Chesapeake Bay. Protecting the surrounding land therefore helps maintain areas that contribute to groundwater and surface-water systems, while also retaining habitat for wildlife.Biddle has long described seeing bears, turkeys, deer and waterfowl around his home. The conservation agreement ensures that those wooded areas and open fields will remain part of the landscape rather than being converted into a residential development.A partnership behind the preservationThe Centre County Farmland Trust worked with ClearWater Conservancy to complete the project. ClearWater assisted with mapping, fieldwork and technical and legal aspects of establishing the easement. For Biddle, however, the preservation process had been decades in the making. The farm had also spent time on the county’s waiting list for agricultural conservation through the Purchase of Agricultural Conservation Easement Program.The new easement does not end farming on the property. Instead, it separates the future of the farm from the possibility of development. That matters because Biddle’s own future on the land is uncertain. He has acknowledged that finding the next generation of farmers is difficult, particularly because of the capital required to start and operate a farm.But regardless of who eventually works the fields, the basic character of Bear Meadows has now been secured: 170 acres where farmland, forest, wildlife and water can continue to exist without being replaced by development.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ms Rachel says she won’t work with ‘privileged’ people who stay silent on Gaza
articles.summary: Ms. Rachel declared she won't work with "privileged" people silent on Gaza, prompting Campaign Against Antisemitism to call it exclusionary.
articles.body: Children’s entertainer Ms. Rachel said she would not work with "privileged" people who have remained silent about civilians in Gaza, drawing criticism Tuesday from Campaign Against Antisemitism over what the group called an exclusionary "political purity test." In a recent Guardian interview, Rachel Griffin Accurso, known online as Ms. Rachel, said she would make an exception for people who could jeopardize their ability to support themselves by speaking publicly, but not those she considers privileged. "I’m going to work with people who aren’t in a privileged position, because that’s not fair to them if they could lose the ability to put food on the table. But people who are privileged who don’t say anything? Yeah, I’m not interested in working with them. Because I feel like maybe if we all said something, the genocide would stop," Accurso said. MS RACHEL SAYS BACKLASH OVER HER GAZA POSTS 'DOESN'T FAZE' HER AS SHE CALLS OUT CELEBRITY SILENCE Campaign Against Antisemitism, which has previously criticized Accurso’s Gaza activism, told Fox News Digital that her distinction failed to account for people who may hold different views on the Israel-Hamas war, including Jewish colleagues. "Ms Rachel’s comments on who she is willing to work with are patently hypocritical. Acting as an adjudicator is a privileged position in and of itself, and subjecting people to political purity tests is by definition exclusionary," the spokesperson said. "One would have thought that someone who has admitted to having – apparently accidentally – liked a comment online saying, ‘Free America from the Jews’, Ms Rachel would be taking care to avoid these sorts of topics entirely." "Evidently the temptation to ostracize those with differing views on the war in Gaza, many of whom will be Jews, is too strong for her to resist," the spokesperson added. MS RACHEL CONFRONTED ON ACCUSING ISRAEL OF 'GENOCIDE' IN PARK INTERACTION WITH PODCASTER Accurso's comments followed a series of public challenges to wealthy celebrities over Gaza. During a recent appearance on comedian Ilana Glazer's "It's Open" podcast, she questioned why celebrities whose careers were secure would not risk speaking publicly. "If you are so famous, and you’re uncancellable, and you’re so famous, and you won’t even say like, ‘Kids in Gaza should have schools, people in Gaza should have hospitals.’ Like you won't say something so basic and like why can't you risk something to help save lives?" Accurso said. Accurso also recently pledged to match rapper Macklemore’s $1 million donation to Palestinian aid organizations and called on "every wealthy White celebrity" to do the same, Fox News Digital reported. KAROL MARKOWICZ: MS. RACHEL SAID, 'I AM POLITICAL.' PARENTS SHOULD TAKE HER AT HER WORD Her remarks about who she is willing to work with came as Accurso has repeatedly framed her advocacy as concern for children regardless of nationality or religion. In the Guardian interview, she addressed criticism of her focus on Gaza. "I was confused and devastated that people said because you care about children who are starving, and whose food is being blocked, you don’t care about these [Jewish] kids," Accurso said. "I was like, oh my gosh, I have a deep love for, a deep care for, all children." Accurso also recently faced scrutiny over her ties to Palestinian photojournalist Motaz Azaiza after a 2025 video resurfaced showing her introducing him to her young audience as her "friend." The clip resurfaced days after Azaiza said in a podcast interview that he filmed Israeli hostages being beaten by a crowd in Gaza on Oct. 7, 2023, but deliberately withheld the footage. articles.title: Wyoming man kicks mountain lion in the face to save his dog, then fights it off bare-handed
articles.summary: Adam Borkhus kicked a mountain lion in the face to save his dog Diesel near Cody, Wyoming, but the predator then pounced and knocked him down.
articles.body: Earlier this month, a Wyoming man found himself in a situation no dog owner ever wants to imagine. His Labrador was being attacked by a mountain lion. So he did the only thing he could think to do. He kicked the big cat in the face. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS Adam Borkhus, a 33-year-old amateur wildlife photographer, was out looking for elk near Cody, Wyo., on Sept. 19 when he stopped along a remote road to change camera lenses and let his 2-year-old Lab, Diesel, out of the vehicle. Seconds later, he heard his dog yelp. Borkhus ran into the brush and found a mountain lion on top of Diesel. He had both a firearm and bear spray with him, but with his dog tangled up with the cat, he didn't want to risk hitting Diesel with either. So Borkhus went with Plan C: his foot. A swift kick square in the mountain lion’s face successfully got the cat off Diesel. Unfortunately, it also got the cat's attention. "The lion spun around and looked at me," Borkhus told Outside. "Then it pounced and hit me in the chest." Borkhus — who stands 6-foot-3 and weighs roughly 300 pounds — was knocked onto his back by the approximately 70-pound cat. He said he tried to keep its teeth away from his face and neck while punching it with his free hand before eventually grabbing its ear and wrenching it hard enough that the lion took off. The whole thing lasted somewhere around 20 to 30 seconds. Borkhus escaped with scratches to his hands, arm and face. Diesel somehow came out of the ordeal without any injuries. And, while his owner was busy throwing hands with a mountain lion, he retreated to the vehicle. BIG SKY, MONTANA WILDLIFE ENCOUNTER CAUGHT ON VIDEO AS MOOSE CHARGES TOWARD WOMAN AND HER DOGS He was waiting for Borkhus at the tailgate. Not much of a protective instinct there, but we’re sure Diesel is still a good boy anyway. What should you actually do if you encounter a mountain lion? Kicking a mountain lion in the face worked out remarkably well for Borkhus. But it probably shouldn't be your first line of defense. Wyoming Game and Fish says conflicts between humans and mountain lions are rare, but there are several things people should know when recreating in lion country. For starters, don't approach one — which should be obvious. Give the animal room to escape and remain calm if you encounter one. The department recommends speaking calmly and firmly rather than running away. Traveling in groups can also reduce the chances of surprising a mountain lion in the first place. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER And if things go sideways? Fight back. That's the official advice from Wyoming Game and Fish: "If a mountain lion attacks you, fight back and defend yourself." Outside also spoke with Mountain Lion Foundation researcher Joshua Lisbon, who recommended keeping dogs leashed or under strong voice control while in the wilderness. If a lion does grab your dog, Lisbon recommends using bear spray rather than physically jumping into the fight — even if your dog gets sprayed in the process. Obviously, that's much easier advice to process while sitting safely at home than when your best friend is underneath a mountain lion. But thank goodness for Borkhus and Diesel, it worked out this time. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Love all things wildlife and outdoors? Follow OutKick OutDoors on Instagram and TikTok!

articles.title: More than 400 detained as France student protests escalate
articles.summary: Students have been protesting conditions and resources in high schools since last week.
articles.body:
More than 400 people, mostly minors, were detained in France on Tuesday over student protests at high schools across the country, the French interior minister said.

The demonstrations, which began in Paris and have seen teenagers blockade their schools for days, stem from issues including overcrowded classes and teacher shortages.

At least 10 teachers and several students, as well as 48 law enforcement officials, were injured during Tuesday's protests, officials said. According to the education ministry, at least 400 schools were affected.

Pictures and videos appeared to show bins being set alight and bus stops damaged by protesters.

"We're here to deliver a message," one 16-year-old female student told the AFP news agency. "We're not here to smash everything up for no reason. We're here precisely to say that the education system is completely broken. There are 34 of us in each class, and it's just not feasible. The teachers are overworked."

Taking to X, French Education Minister Édouard Geffray said students have the right to protest, but condemned reports of violence as "indefensible".

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told BFMTV 440 people were detained, adding: "We don't have the final tally yet, but I'm told two thirds led to police custody."

French media reported that protesters hurled projectiles at police, who responded with batons and tear gas.

Speaking to AFP, Ryad Rani, president of Union Syndicale Lycéenne, which represents students, accused the French government of "repression" and police of using excessive force.

When pressed on the police response to the protests, which has been criticised by several French politicians, Nuñez said it had been "carried out in an extremely proportionate manner".

Writing on social media on Tuesday evening, education minister Geffray said: "The right to demonstrate is a fundamental freedom that cannot serve as an excuse for such actions.

"To legitimise them or, in this context, to call for extending the blockades is to endanger our students as well as public employees. It is irresponsible."

The movement at French lycées, equivalent to sixth form in the UK or high school in the US, began last week in the Île-de-France region around Paris.

On Monday, France's Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu warned any escalation in the student protests would be "irresponsible" following the arrest of 164 people.

Lecornu cited reported incidents at protests in a post on X, saying: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers."

The continuing student demonstrations on Tuesday coincided with nationwide walkouts by unions representing teachers, hospital staff and civil servants to protest against issues including low wages and working conditions.

Nuñez said these protests, with at least 200,000 participants reported, mostly went without incident.

articles.title: 'Operate faster than adversary': CDS Gen Subramani stresses integrated multi-domain ops
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Chief of defence staff General NS Raja Subramani said on Tuesday, “operate faster in various domains than the adversary can respond and create
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Chief of defence staff General NS Raja Subramani said on Tuesday, “operate faster in various domains than the adversary can respond and create problems for you”.India’s military transformation must move from buying individual platforms to building an integrated, sovereign, data-driven “system of systems”, supported by resilient networks, AI, digital engineering and faster industry-led innovation. It is time for the transformation of India’s armed forces from platform-centric warfare to integrated, data-centric multi-domain operations, he said.At the Defence Tech Summit on 'Multi-Domain Defence Capability Development and Digital Engineering', organised by the Centre for Emerging Technologies at USI, Gen Subramani said resilient communications will determine operational effectiveness. He highlighted that space-based assets alone are insufficient. They must communicate with aerial, naval, ground and electronic-warfare assets in near real time, and this requires resilient communications capable of surviving an electronically contested environment, he said.CDS stressed that future capability planning should not begin with what the Army, Navy or Air Force individually wants. It should begin with the effect that needs to be created on the battlefield, he said. Space, air, naval, land, electronic-warfare and other assets must therefore operate as an integrated system, with sensors able to detect a target, share information and enable an appropriate response across domains, he emphasised.According to CDS, India has made considerable progress in building defence networks, but the next phase is about the data flowing over those networks, and the armed forces must break down data silos. One of his observations was that the services must move away from the tendency to “jealously guard” their data. Existing paper-based information should be digitised, and sharing should become the default wherever operationally feasible, he stressed.India needs sovereign and purpose-specific AI models, he said, acknowledging that the country is not yet at the level of the leading frontier AI models. He suggested a pragmatic two-track approach: use and train appropriate open-source models within secure networks, while developing sovereign or purpose-specific language models for sensitive and high-security applications. AI adoption is unavoidable, but command must remain human, he said, adding that no military force can remain competitive without adopting AI, but the ultimate decision must remain with the commander.In a direct message to the industry, CDS said the industry needs to deliver “volume, scale and speed”.Talking about USI, Subramani said, “It's my proud privilege to be here. I was, as General Pawan Anand mentioned, around a year and a half back when we started this session. I must confess that having associated with the USI has also improved my technological knowledge, strategic knowledge, and geopolitical knowledge. And I must also compliment Admiral SJ Singh and General Pawan Anand for really taking the USI work several notches higher.”

articles.title: In 2009, two former Royal Marines rowed from Japan to San Francisco; 189 days and almost 7,000 miles later they set a Pacific record
articles.summary: For months, the Pacific offered Mick Dawson and Chris Martin little indication that their destination was getting any closer.
articles.body: For months, the Pacific offered Mick Dawson and Chris Martin little indication that their destination was getting any closer. They left Choshi (Japan), in a small rowing boat in 2009, expecting a long passage across one of the world's largest stretches of open water. Instead, wind and currents repeatedly pushed them away from their intended line. By the time they finally reached San Francisco, their route had stretched to almost 7,000 miles. They had spent 189 days at sea, rowing in shifts, sleeping in a cramped cabin and living largely on freeze-dried food. According to Reuters, the pair passed beneath the Golden Gate Bridge completing a journey that Dawson had already attempted twice on his own.Dawson’s failed Pacific attempts led to a new boat with Chris MartinFor Dawson, the crossing was tied to several earlier attempts to travel between Japan and California by rowing boat. The former Royal Marine and professional yacht skipper had already crossed the Atlantic twice, first with his brother Steve in 2001 and again in 2005 with Andrew Morris.The North Pacific had proved considerably less forgiving. Dawson first tried the Japan-to-San Francisco route alone in 2003, but severe weather tore away his rudder and forced him to abandon the attempt and return to Japan. He tried again the following year in 2004. That voyage ended after 109 days when his boat capsized and sank, despite having covered more than 4,500 miles.Rather than leave the route behind, Dawson designed another boat for the specific demands of the Pacific. He called it ‘Bojangles’ and brought Chris Martin, a fellow ocean rower and friend, into the project.Bojangles became a tiny home for the pair on their Pacific journeyReuters reported, the pair departed from Choshi, near Tokyo, in May 2009. Bojangles was about 23 feet, or seven metres, long, with a layout that allowed the men to row together or separately. Their daily routine revolved around two-hour periods of rowing and sleep. The compact cabin at one end provided their sleeping space, while the other section carried food, communications equipment and the machinery needed to turn seawater into drinking water.They had hoped to complete the voyage without outside assistance. That plan held for most of the crossing, but food eventually became a problem. With California about 100 miles away, the men ran short of supplies and accepted a helicopter drop of provisions. The intervention meant the voyage was not entirely unassisted, although the pair continued under their own power towards the coast.A 4,600-mile journey became a far longer battle against the PacificThe distance between Japan and San Francisco is roughly 4,600 miles by the more direct ocean passage. Their actual journey was far longer. Winds and currents repeatedly altered the course of Bojangles, leaving the rowers dealing with a route that expanded towards 7,000 miles. Near the end, their plotted track formed a large loop in the Pacific rather than a straightforward line towards California.Martin, who was 28 at the time, later recalled how frustrating it became to watch the remaining distance fail to fall as expected. The boat could be moving for hours while the figures on their navigation chart seemed barely to change.The conditions also shifted with the seasons. They had started in relatively warm weather and initially rowed without clothes, but the final part of the journey brought colder conditions and more difficult weather.Life inside a small ocean-going boatBojangles gave the two men enough room to operate but little space for comfort. Its design was closer to a large ocean-going rowing craft than a conventional boat, with seats on rollers allowing the rowers to bring their legs into each stroke. They alternated between rowing and sleeping, meaning that neither man followed a normal day-night routine. Food was mostly freeze-dried, while a desalination system supplied drinking water from the surrounding ocean.Technology was another part of the expedition. The pair carried equipment to document the journey and publish updates, giving people on land a view of what was happening far offshore. The physical surroundings, however, remained simple. There was the boat, the ocean, their equipment and whatever weather came across the Pacific.The final approach to San FranciscoBy the time the California coastline came within reach, the men had spent more than six months at sea. The journey that began in Choshi had become a 189-day passage, with the additional distance caused by the diversions making the final approach especially prolonged. According to Reuters, on the morning of November 13, 2009, Bojangles entered San Francisco Bay. At about 8:30 am, the pair passed beneath the Golden Gate Bridge.They marked the moment in a simple way, opening beers as they reached the bay. Soon afterwards they were at the Golden Gate Yacht Club, where the change from a restricted diet at sea to substantial meals was hard to miss. Both had lost considerable weight during the crossing.A Pacific record after earlier failuresDawson and Martin became the first crew to row successfully from Choshi in Japan to the Golden Gate Bridge. According to the official 189 days website, their recorded passage lasted 189 days, 10 hours and 55 minutes, covering roughly 7,000 miles rather than the much shorter direct distance between the two points.For Dawson, the arrival also closed a chapter that had included two unsuccessful solo attempts at the same crossing. The first had ended with a damaged rudder. The second had ended when his boat sank after a capsize.This time, Bojangles carried two rowers all the way across. The route was longer than planned, the food eventually ran short and the weather became harsher towards California, but the boat reached San Francisco under the pair's own rowing effort.You use AI every day. articles.title: US Supreme Court allows Trump to continue third-country deportations
articles.summary: The high court grants an emergency petition ahead of expected arguments in the case, slated for December.
articles.body:
The United States Supreme Court has allowed President Donald Trump’s administration to continue third-country deportations, halting a lower-court ruling that paused such removals over questions of due process.

On Tuesday, the high court granted the administration’s emergency request to resume the deportations, which involve sending immigrants to countries they may have no connection to.

The court’s order was unsigned, as is typical for an emergency petition. It also does not include an explanation or a list of how the justices voted.

But at the bottom of Tuesday’s order, the court’s three left-leaning justices – Sonia Sotomayor, Ketanji Brown Jackson and Elena Kagan – indicated they would have denied the Trump administration’s petition.

The Supreme Court’s decision to pause the lower court ruling is temporary. The order calls for arguments to be heard in December.

That hearing comes as Trump administration continues its appeal against the lower court’s ruling, handed down by Judge Brian Murphy in Boston, Massachusetts.

Murphy had ruled that immigrants must be given a “meaningful” chance to raise safety concerns before their removal to third-party countries.

In pausing such deportations, Murphy indicated that some immigrants may have been denied the opportunity to challenge their deportations as part of their due process rights.

Tuesday, however, is not the first time the Supreme Court justices have weighed in on the practice of forcibly sending people to third countries, which Trump dramatically stepped up since his return to office in 2025.

Trump campaigned on a pledge to implement the “largest deportation operation in American history”, and his officials have argued that third-country deportations are a means of removing individuals whose home countries may not accept them.

In June 2025, the Supreme Court also issued an unsigned order allowing such removals to proceed.

That cleared the way for eight men, including nationals of Cuba, Myanmar and Vietnam, to be deported to South Sudan , a country the US State Department advises against visiting because of “crime, kidnapping, and armed conflict”.

The Department of Homeland Security at the time called the removals “a win”, while rights groups said the move flouted basic legal protections.

Critics have expressed concern that many of the governments receiving third-country deportations have a record of human rights abuses.

Third-country deportations have been used to bypass court protection orders that prevent immigrants from being sent back to their home countries due to fears of persecution.

But advocates say that some of those third-party countries have ultimately sent deportees, including asylum seekers, back to the places where they feared they would be at risk of torture or other harms.

At least 35 countries have signed agreements with the Trump administration to take in the third-country nationals, according to a tally by the nonprofits Refugees International and Human Rights First.

The groups estimate that more than 25,000 people have been subject to third-country deportations so far.

On Monday, human rights experts at the United Nations wrote to the ‌US ‌government urging a halt to such removals, warning they were putting deportees at heightened risk of abuse.

“At gravest risk are children, women, persons with disabilities, victims of trafficking, LGBT persons, human rights defenders, stateless persons and other people in extremely vulnerable situations,” the experts said.

On Tuesday, Burundi became the latest country to enter an agreement with the US to take non-citizen deportations.

Officials said the country would only take in people who were not facing prosecution and had no links to “terrorism”.
